name: Bishop's Purple
lede: Bishop's Purple is a muted, reddish purple from Robert Ridgway's 1912 color dictionary, and it is one of the rarest colors in our painting archive.

sections.title: A title, not a named man
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 “Color Standards and Color Nomenclature” lists Bishop's Purple at hex #9B688B among the names he credits to a person [1]. Here the word is a church office rather than a surname, and Ridgway does not say which bishop, or whose vestments, he had in mind, so the connection is undocumented in our sources [1]. The 1955 Inter-Society Color Council catalog repeats the name in the block it calls moderate reddish purple [1].

Its nearest neighbor in our color graph is [[antique-fuchsia|Antique Fuchsia]], 4.4 units away and darker [1]. [[light-perilla-purple|Light Perilla Purple]] and [[aconite-violet|Aconite Violet]] sit just beyond that, both redder [1]. Against the basic color words it reads closest to [[mauve|Mauve]], 6.1 units off, though Bishop's Purple carries more grey and less pink [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive matches this purple in only 0.03% of 23,781 paintings, 6 of them, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in just 1 [2]. That makes it rarer than 86% of the named colors in our set, too thin a sample for a reliable century, painter or country figure [2]. The handful of matches we do have run from 1889 to 1892, among them a work by Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, but with so few paintings this is a curiosity, not a trend, and every figure here is a computed color match in an aged photograph, not proof of a pigment or dye [2].
